title: Ksitigarbha's vow
hookLine: the bodhisattva vows not to rest until the hell realms are empty

lines: A PROMISE WITH NO END IN SIGHT.
cards: Until the hells are empty, I will not become a Buddha. That's the vow, in the short form it's carried in, of a bodhisattva named Ksitigarbha.
A promise usually comes with an end in sight: until the project's done, until the kids are grown, until the debt is paid. This one is built so that the end may never come.
And the one who made it, in the story his sutra tells, started out as a grieving daughter.

teach.h: A DAUGHTER FEARS FOR HER MOTHER.
teach.b: The Sutra of Ksitigarbha's Original Vows tells several stories of his past lives. Here's one. Long ago, in the time of an earlier Buddha, there lived a young woman of a brahmin family, devoted and kind.
Her mother was not. Her mother mocked the teaching and the Buddha, and then she died. The daughter was afraid of where her mother's actions would carry her.
So she sold what she had, made offerings, and gave herself to devotion to the Buddha of that age, calling on him with her whole heart.
In the sutra's telling, she was taken to the edge of the hell realms, a sea of suffering, and she saw what was there.
A guardian told her that her mother had already been freed, because of the merit of her daughter's devotion. Her mother was safe. Here's the turn.
She didn't go home relieved. She had seen everyone else still down there.
So she vowed, before that Buddha, to spend lifetimes freeing every being who suffered in those places. That young woman, the sutra says, became Ksitigarbha.
A private grief, for one person, opens out into a promise for everyone. He's the bodhisattva who goes down into the lowest places, the ones others would rather not look at.

teach.h: A STAFF, AND A LIGHT IN THE DARK.
teach.b: In art he's often a monk with a shaved head, holding a staff with rings and a jewel; some say the staff opens the gates and the jewel lights up the dark.
Some read the vow as holding back his own awakening. Others hear that his awakening and everyone else's are tied together, and he won't untie them.

how: In Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and Japanese Buddhism, Ksitigarbha is honored as the bodhisattva of the lower realms, and his sutra is often recited for parents and loved ones who have died.

games.q: you're the young woman. a guardian at the edge of the hells tells you your mother is already free. what do you do?
o: vow to free every being still suffering there.
ask to see your mother first.
games.why: she vows to spend lifetimes freeing all who suffer there. the sutra says that young woman became Ksitigarbha.

practice: Bring to mind someone in a place most people would rather not look at: a person sleeping in a doorway, someone in prison, a relative the family has stopped calling.
Notice the pull to look away, and don't fight it; just come back and stay with them for one more breath, then another.

wordCard.voice: Ksitigarbha's vow. The bodhisattva's promise not to become a Buddha until the hell realms are empty. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit name of the bodhisattva, usually rendered earth store or earth womb.

carryVoice: Your line: not until all are free. If grief is heavy for you today, you don't have to carry it alone: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help. Twelve hundred days.
